title: Valheim 1.0 review
summary: Your long journey is at an end, Viking.
body: Need to know What is it? A Viking-themed survival game set in a procedurally generated open world. Release date : September 09, 2026 (1.0) Expect to pay : $30/£23.49 [Remember: if the price is 49.99, round it up to 50.] Developer : Iron Gate AB Publisher : Coffee Stain Publishing Reviewed on : Intel i7 9700K, RTX 4070 Ti, 16GB RAM Steam Deck : Verified Link : Official site After a day-long battle with one of Valheim's big bosses, I return to my modest cabin in the woods to recover. I'm exhausted, my weapons and armor are mostly broken, and I've burned through my meager supply of food and arrows. I don't even have a spare torch left to light my way home. Even though I was victorious, the cold and rainy night doesn't put me in the mood for a celebration. Then I spot a shadowy figure in the gloom, leaning on a walking stick, one blue eye gleaming from beneath its hood. Odin . It's frickin' Odin himself, y'know, Thor's dad? He's visiting the exiled tenth world of Valheim to peep me in person. Suddenly my mood lifts and I feel like a complete badass. Odin knows who I am. This isn't my first visitation from the ancient god: I've been playing Valheim since its early access release in 202…

SteelSeries throws everything but the kitchen sink in the feature list of its Aeon Pro controller
summary: It can seamlessly switch between Xbox and PC, but is very expensive.
body: Last month I got to take a look at what SteelSeries calls the "world’s first dual-dock controller built for PC and Xbox": the Aeon Pro. Its dual-docking claim to fame is that it allows you to switch between PC and Xbox gameplay seamlessly, without re-pairing. That's thanks to dual USB inputs on the base station, one connected to PC and the other to Xbox. The thing is, that feature itself sounds pretty niche to my diminutive ears, given there probably aren't tons of PC gamers also using Xbox (though I am open to being corrected on that). Instead, I'm much more interested in what else the controller has to offer, and for what cost. On this front, we're looking at a *gulp* $260/£230/€260 price tag, which places it firmly in top-end territory at least as far as its pricing is concerned. Having had my hands on it—albeit only briefly—I can say it does feel like a premium controller, with pretty solid build quality, great grips, and comfy button presses. I'm not a fan of the ABXY buttons, however, as they feel slightly mushy for my tastes, but only in the same way that some other premium controllers are and that others seem to not mind. For me, it feel like there's a bit of slow pre-trav…

title: Sources say another 10% price increase for Intel CPUs is on the way, and it could be here as soon as October
summary: Up, up, and away.
body: The price of Intel CPUs may be about to increase by a further 10%. Processors, as with almost all things hardware, have been steadily climbing in price since the end of 2025. This latest price increase for Intel CPUs looks set to take effect from October 5, this year. A number of lower-core product lines will also be nearing end-of-life, according to supply chain sources that spoke to DigiTimes . It remains unclear which processors will be impacted in either case. This follows last month's report of a desktop CPU sales slump for both Intel and AMD . The most recent Intel price increases affecting PC gamers were for the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus and the Core 5 250K Plus . Part of the continuing upward trend can be blamed on increasing prices for PCBs, which is also having a knock-on effect on motherboard prices . The memory supply crisis also doesn't help. But additionally, sources say Intel CEO Chen Liwu is looking into the CPU segment of the business anyway, reviewing pricing and profit. Speaking of restructuring, though, DigiTimes' sources also claim that there will be further layoffs at Intel. It's rumoured the company could lose between 5 and 10% of its current work force, and th…

title: Don't Nod might not have enough cash to make it through January 2027, and even if it does, pulling up could 'involve the reduction of up to 90 positions'
summary: "Amid systemic pressures in the video game industry."
body: Don't Nod, best known as the developers of Life is Strange 1 and 2, has been having a rough go of it, lately. In 2024, its games Jusant and Banishers: Ghosts of New Eden sold "well below expectations" , causing it to pause development of two further games. Then, in 2025, it laid off several employees after Lost Records didn't quite make up the difference. Based on this financial update (thanks, GamesIndustry.biz ), its third-person adventure game Aphelion didn't pull things back from the brink, either. The developer reported a 56% decrease in operating revenue year-on-year, "amid systemic pressures in the video game industry, characterized by highly selective financing." This also presented as a €3.5 million decline in sales in the first half of 2026, "driven primarily by sales and the recognition of a portion of PS+ and Game Pass revenue from Bloom and Rage, initial sales of Aphelion, and the back catalog", as well as an increase development costs to the tune of €2.6 million because of an as-yet-unannounced collaboration with Netflix for "a narrative game based on a major Netflix intellectual property." This is a dire forecast, as it means there's a "material uncertainty regardin…

title: Valve appears to implementing a reservation system for the Steam Frame, suggesting it expects demand will outstrip supply at launch
summary: Closer than you think.
body: A release date for the Steam Frame has not yet been officially announced. However, data mining by VR leaker Brad Lynch has unearthed a reservation system in Valve's back-end, suggesting the hardware may not be far off. Lynch shared a look at the definitely not yet live reservation system on X . "Expect nothing. It isn’t ready," he posted, accompanied by a screenshot of a lottery drawing notification email claiming the draw results would be revealed on the placeholder date of 31 December, 1969. Obviously, Valve aren't time travellers, and this date was likely chosen to avoid any part of this system going live before it's meant to. Lynch wrote that the reservation system "is already up in Steam's backend for these two SKUs" in an earlier post , but shared no further hardware details. The data miner then added, "Before you ask: No. You can’t do anything with this information to beat the lottery system." A reservation system isn't all that surprising, as Valve had these in place for both the Steam Machine and the new Steam Controller . The queue appears to have shortened for the Steam Machine since its June release, but Valve likely won't catch up on new Steam Controller reservations …

title: Persona 1 and 2 remakes are something Atlus will 'probably eventually do', which is great, but the PS2-era Shin Megami Tensei games are sitting right there
summary: Prioritize what I in particular want first, please Atlus.
body: Atlus will probably remake Persona 1 and 2 one day, according to a new interview with series producer Kazuhisa Wada conducted by Rock Paper Shotgun . "For me, I think a remaster or remake is some kind of cultural preservation," Wada said. "As a creator, it’s your duty to take the things you’ve done and make sure they’re not lost, and are still around in the modern day. From that same perspective, Persona 1 and 2 are something we’ll probably eventually do too.” Persona Revelations was released on the original PlayStation in 1996. It's actually been lightly reissued before, in 2009 for the PlayStation Portable, and surprisingly, there's even a 1999 PC port that was never released in the west. While it focuses on a cast of school students, the social links system—arguably the series' best trick—wasn't introduced to the series until Persona 3. It's the Persona game that feels closest to the older Shin Megami Tensei games, since it has first-person blobber-style dungeon exploration, though overworld exploration is conducted via an isometric third-person perspective. Persona 2: Innocent Sin released in 1999, also for the original PlayStation. It replaces first-person dungeon crawling wi…

title: Capcom expresses continued interest in 're-activating IPs' as the first new Onimusha game in 20 years surpasses 1 million sales on launch day
summary: Onimusha: Way of the Sword's launch day success has propelled the series to 10 million lifetime sales, says Capcom.
body: Samurai adventure Onimusha: Way of the Sword notched over a million sales on its launch day, Capcom has announced. The success is deserved, per our reviewer Wes, who said that Way of the Sword "whips ass" in his 83/100 review . (And if the demo had you worried that it wouldn't be much of a challenge, Wes says not to fret too much: "I died plenty, particularly to bosses that ruthlessly punished my poor parry timing or overeager button mashing.") According to Capcom, the one million launch day sales for Way of the Sword has put the Onimusha series as a whole at 10 million lifetime sales. The last new game in the main series was Onimusha: Dawn of Dreams, which released 20 years ago. "In addition to regularly releasing major new titles each year, Capcom is focusing on re-activating IPs that haven't had a new title launch recently," the developer said. "The company is working to further maximize corporate value by leveraging its rich library of content, including this title." New Lost Planet game when? It's become a cliche to say that Capcom's on a bit of a run lately, but here's yet another mile marker in the developer's 2020s streak, which has included a pair of well-liked Resident E…

title: Scuf Omega review
summary: Closer to an Alpha or Beta than an Omega.
body: In recent years, Scuf controllers have lost some of their purpose to me. I distinctly remember wanting a Scuf controller to play Call of Duty as a teenager, as they were one of the only brands making solid pro controllers with distinct visuals and partnership deals with pro players. Now, you can get a pro controller from most major gaming brands, like Asus, Turtle Beach, and Razer, and you can even get cheaper pro controllers from the likes of GameSir. As such, it's no longer good enough to just offer a few extra buttons; you need to do something truly unique… or truly affordable. The Scuf Omega attempts the former and gets no way near the latter. Its central selling point is dual compatibility with PC and PlayStation, plus some extra triggers on the grips. But things have changed in recent years, and it needs strong build quality, great feel, and a host of other features to really justify that price. Buy if… ✅ You want a PS5 controller built for PC: The Scuf Omega is the closest I've felt to Sony's DualSense not made by Sony. Do not buy if… ❌ You won't use it on PS5: If you simply want a PC pro controller, there are much stronger choices from Scuf's competition. Features Scuf Ome…

title: Square Enix wants Final Fantasy 7 to be an 'IP with an ever-evolving future', which is strange to say about a franchise that's already ever-evolving
summary: But hey, everyone loves Cloud, so.
body: Final Fantasy 7's remake trilogy has, at the very least, given us a trio of pretty solid RPGs—I had a great time with the first, and I'm soon to buckle up and finally give Rebirth a go. But I can't help but wonder, quietly, whether or not Final Fantasy has fallen into the same 'fear of new IP trap' as other games. That's not to say that the FF series isn't getting new games. Final Fantasy 16 came out in 2023 and snagged a solid 79 from us in our Final Fantasy 16 review . And yet, a small part of me wonders what new and exciting games we might've gotten if Square Enix had devoted the Remake team to making new final fantasies, rather than spending three entire big-budget titles and over half a decade rehashing a classic. And yet, Square seems reluctant to release its grip over the FF7 cast. That's per a PAX West panel (thanks, GamesRadar+ ) wherein director Naoki Hamaguchi said (via translator): "We want to make this a work that creates new fans 20 or even 30 years from now," a game that can "move beyond being a classic of the past and shape it into an IP with an ever-evolving future." And listen, I don't want to be a grumpy old git about this, but… that's just what Final Fantasy is…

title: Steam Week in Review: 54 idle games released on Steam last week, and many look eerily similar
summary: All the interesting Steam facts for the week ending September 6.
body: When Cookie Clicker and Candy Box both released in quick succession in 2013, I remember them being received mostly as a joke, or else as an amusing parody of "watch numbers go up" RPG gameplay. Then something weird happened: all my colleagues became fixated on Cookie Clicker. So did I. Lots of people on the internet, on Twitter and in various forums like Reddit, confessed to having become addicted to it. Cookie Clicker did have an antecedent in Ian Bogost's Cow Clicker, which was a very deliberate satire . But Cookie Clicker wasn't presented as satire. And yet, it was so transparently meaningless that people doubted it could be anything else. You click a cookie repeatedly to generate more cookies. Once you earn enough cookies, you can invest those cookies into various ways of expediting the cookie making process. You click and watch numbers go up. It's stupid. Fast forward more than a decade later and idlers, also known as incremental games, are massive on Steam. Last week, 54 games with the tag "idler" released. In total, there are 4,314 games with that tag on Steam. Some of these look pretty good as far as idlers go. Next Reign: Kingdom has pretty handmade pixel art, atmospheric…

title: 'If you're designing an RPG, you have to go back to the source:' The post-apocalyptic RPG Entropy takes notes from Fallout and a long-abandoned Warhammer spinoff
summary: Consulting the foundational texts.
body: The early access RPG Entropy is a very different beast to its developers' previous work. Dread Delusion was a shockingly good homage to first person RPGs like King's Field or The Elder Scrolls, while this new game is distinctly JRPG-inflected, nailing a lot of the feel and intangibles of something like Final Fantasy 10 or Lost Odyssey. But you can't just put it into the JRPG bin and call it a day. Entropy boasts a large party size for tactical battles, permadeath, locational damage, as well as an approach to reactivity and storytelling that feels more PC gaming than PS2 gaming. When I spoke to lead developer James Wragg recently, he told me that's very deliberate. "In many ways, if Dread Delusion was my take on The Elder Scrolls, then this is my take on Fallout," Wragg said. "The original Fallout, Fallout 1, is one of my favorite games, and we're riffing on that quite a lot with Entropy." Having played Entropy's demo and a bit of early access, I immediately got what he meant. Part of that inspiration is visible in the locational damage system, similar to OG Fallout's called shots (what would eventually become VATS in the 3D games). You can incur a penalty to accuracy to target a s…

title: A hobby dev built a free, 3D galaxy map for Warhammer 40K that loads like lightning in your browser
summary: I just think it's neat.
body: Sometimes it's nice to just find something cool and fun and free on the internet, and the Cartographia Imperialis is just that: A 3D galaxy map of the Warhammer 40K Milky Way you can peruse in your browser. It has the same simple, awe-inspiring majesty as Mass Effect's take on the concept, and you can explore it like an isometric videogame: Left click and drag to pan around, right click to rotate the camera, mouse wheel to zoom in and out. You can click on notable planets or regions to get little lore entries, or pull 'em up by name in the index to snap straight there on the map. I'm not sure where creator Sami Gashi sourced the text for entries, pulling straight from official sources or paraphrasing in their own words, but I quite like the very in-universe prose. Take the entry for largely-unremarkable hive world Jouran, for example: "Its dossier is a reminder that strategic maps hide ordinary misery behind a clean point of light," the entry reads. "Jouran's value lies in quotas met, bodies counted, and local authorities willing to preserve output by any sanctioned means." That's good stuff. Perhaps best of all, Cartographia Imperialis is completely free with no ads, and the map …

body: On September 5, Rebel Wolves took to Twitter on the official Blood of Dawnwalker account to announce that the dark vampire RPG had already surpassed one million copies sold just three days after its September 2 launch. "Thank you for playing, sharing, supporting, and being part of the community," the developer wrote in its celebratory post . I was in a Star Wars Zero Company-shaped hole during Dawnwalker's contemporaneous review period, but everyone on our team who played has been pretty pleased with this very Witcher-like RPG from ex-Witcher devs. Australian editor Shaun Prescott awarded it an 83% in his review , praising the storytelling and combat, but wishing that Rebel Wolves had gone harder on Dawnwalker's unique time mechanics. "Maybe Rebel Wolves worried that too many players would fall afoul of the passage of time and thus loosened its severity." title: Do you ever listen to videogame music in your day-to-day life?
summary: Or should videogame music stay *inside* the game?
body: You know, I do a lot of prattling about videogame music at this humble website PC Gamer dot com. It's practically woven into the fabric of my very being at this point—hugely formative for me growing up, and now I carry little bits of it everywhere. I have half a dozen VGM playlists dedicated to stuff like the gym, relaxing, and locking in at work. I've formed lifelong memories with friends as we've filled karaoke rooms with the sound of all kinds of Final Fantasy 14 tracks, where our so-called tastes in "regular" music might misalign; we're instead united by our mutual love and attachment to the songs we hear in a game. In fact, it's so deeply entrenched into my everyday life that I can't imagine any videogame fan not listening to their favourite tunes outside of the game they came from. That is, until I was recently chatting with a friend where they told me just that: even if they really like a song in a videogame, they'll never go out of their way to listen to it detached from its origin. So that had me wondering—how many of you actually listen to videogame music in your day-to-day life? Does it accompany you while you run errands? Do you have a playlist specifically dedicated t…

title: GSC Game World says there's a reason it didn't give Stalker 2 more time in the oven: 'To make something better, you need to receive feedback, and this feedback should be fresh'
summary: "Every developer would like to have an infinite amount of time, but … the market state is not very promising."
body: Like a lot of survival games, Stalker 2 had a long journey from janky larva to playable, easily recommended butterfly. It's tempting to say that these games ought to just stay under wraps until they're done and relatively bug-free—but at Gamescom 2026, GSC Game World CEO and head of game direction Ievgen Grygorovych told PC Gamer's Joshua Wolens that deciding when to release is a more complex consideration than you might think. As for why the studio didn't just wait to release the game until it was in the state it is now, Grygorovych cited both creative and financial reasons. "To make something better, you need to receive feedback, and this feedback should be fresh. From a business perspective, it's also impossible, because it's very expensive to do two years of additional work … in most cases, it's unrealistic." GSC Game World has more legitimate reasons than most to release an unfinished game. The Ukrainian studio was working on Stalker 2 when development was interrupted by Russia's invasion , forcing the team to move out of Kyiv, and its progress was later hamstrung by a devastating office fire and numerous leaks . And notably, the game's buggy release did arrive after delays —…

title: Onimusha: Way of the Sword proves the parry formula is far from stale, you just need to get freaky with it
summary: Parry fatigue? Not me.
body: Listen, I'll be the first to admit that I'm a little biased towards parry-based action games . Sekiro will forever be my favourite FromSoftware game because of just how excellently it captured the back-and-forth feeling of swordplay, not only with its timed deflection mechanic, but its mandate to have you keep the pressure on. But I appreciate that, for some, parry fatigue might be setting in. My fellow writer Mollie Taylor's sick of it , for instance—and I do understand. I think there are some games which use it as a bit of a crutch, and even the ones that don't can wear out their welcome. Take Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, for instance. I liked it, but I wouldn't want every turn-based RPG I play to have a timed block in it. Still, it's fun to have the occasional one where stats can be overcome with deft enough bumper hands. But to paint every parry-based system with the same brush seems short-sighted to me, because this deceptively simple mechanic has a ton of juice still left inside it: no other game proves this more than Onimusha: Way of the Sword, which, as far as I'm concerned, has broken new ground in terms of what parries can do. Onimusha has one parry button, or at least, …

title: I never thought a fishing sim could be this fun, but How to Fish proves me wrong with its ridiculous physics, killer spider crabs, and classic co-op chaos
summary: I now know How to Fish, kinda.
body: I stand knee deep in a pool of blood. My coworkers, comrades, and friends reduced to food for soulless seagulls. Give a man a fish and he may throw it into the mouth of a weary fisherman, teach a man to fish and he shall bring forth the wrath of a spider crab who knows how to stab you with your own knife. This was my first experience of the new multiplayer fishing sim How to Fish , and now I can see why it's become such a smash-hit among bored and borderline-violent friendship groups. (Image credit: Dazed Games) It has a simple premise: you and up to four friends learn how to fish. The cycle of work involves players buying a basic fishing rod at first, using this to fish for, well, fish and crustaceans, and then beating them to death with your bare knuckles, brass knuckles, or a sick-ass knife. Then you can either eat your catch to replenish your health or hunger or feed it to the lonely fisherman who sits on the dock and gives you coins for your hard work. With the coins gained you can buy more tools to help you fish, like the knife, or supplies which you can use as bait, such as half a hotdog or an empty beer can. When I first woke up on the island I was met with a friendly punc…

title: Blending Deus Ex with Escape from Butcher Bay, Deficit is one of the best-feeling indie immersive sims I've played—even if the stealth system needs serious work
summary: Playing the demo for Deficit was far from a net loss.
body: Immersive sims like Deus Ex and Dishonored are among the hardest kinds of games to make, so I always try to be supportive when an indie developer takes on the absurd challenge of creating one. Yet while there have been some good examples in recent years like Skin Deep and New Blood's early access Thief-like Gloomwood , a lot of the experiments in indie imsim design have been simply too janky for me to enjoy. Part of the problem is I'm a highly tactile player, and my primary concern when playing any game is whether it feels good beneath the fingers. If a game falls at that initial hurdle, then it's likely (though not inevitable) that I'll drop it pretty quickly. Fortunately, I had the opposite experience with Deficit , an indie imsim with such a strong sense of physicality that I kept playing the demo despite some clear issues. Developed by Item42, which previously created the cooperative shooter Perish , Deficit sees you play as a freelance spy in a dilapidated, dystopian world. You're tasked with infiltrating a sprawling fortress known as Hadrian's Wall to steal a device called the Interpolator, on behalf of a nameless client known as, well, The Client. The premise is very Deus E…

title: Civilization 7 will finally enter the atomic age in 2027, via a free update Firaxis says will be 'even bigger in scope' than last year's Test of Time
summary: First expansion "Earthrise" also announced.
body: Despite more than a year of updates and at least one massive overhaul, Civilization 7 remains as stubbornly divisive as ever. May's enormous Test of Time update brought significant mechanical reworks and a fresh influx of players to Firaxis' latest entry in the 4X series. But with Steam reviews still sitting at ' Mixed' , with 51% positive, it ultimately did little to shift player opinion. This is partly because numerous aspects of Civ 7 are still rudimentary compared to previous games, including the ability to wage nuclear war. While Firaxis' latest allows players to drop atom bombs on their enemies via World War 2 bombers, its final, modern age ends in 1950, meaning many advanced technologies, including nuclear submarines and ICBMs, are not featured in the game. Fortunately, this is going to change. Alongside the release of update 1.5.0 —which adds features like improved resource generation and an Earth map where your faction starts at their historically-accurate location—Firaxis outlined its update plans for Civ 7 over the next year. This includes another free update that will finally drag the game into the age of the A-bomb. The update is called Arc of Tomorrow , and Firaxis s…

title: Ex-BioWare designer says doom and gloom about the next Mass Effect is overstated: 'I think that they can do it'
summary: "I think BioWare can do it if we just leave them alone to do what they do best."
body: Given that Anthem and Mass Effect Andromeda were widely considered disappointments, and Dragon Age: The Veilguard had a divisive reception, there's a certain amount of skepticism about the Mass Effect game BioWare is currently working on. Some have even suggested it might not come out at all . Armando Troisi, a cinematic designer on the Mass Effect trilogy and lead cinematic designer on Mass Effect 2, thinks it's all a bit much. "I think BioWare, when they break it down and do that singleplayer, interactive narrative-driven, deep combat, progression-driven game, really, there's nobody that can touch them," Troisi told FRVR . "It's kind of like the [Master] Chief, it's like going on a walkabout and finding themselves and coming back. I think BioWare can do it if we just leave them alone to do what they do best." Troisi said that when he was working at BioWare the studio knew what kind of game it was best at making, and that all they need is to get back to that. "The vision was always clear," he said. "There was a BioWare formula and they were going to iterate on that formula and keep turning out best-in-class cinematic RPGs and that's basically what the mandate was. And then they h…

title: Peak studio Aggro Crab is publishing a sick-looking platformer about a blue collar guy doing dirty work on an alien world
summary: That's what's up.
body: At the Game Developers Conference earlier this year, Aggro Crab developer Nick Kaman told me that he thinks there's a lot of meat left on the bone when it comes to co-op " friendslop " games, and that he wants to keep working in the space. Aggro Crab is still down to zig and not zag, though, and will be publishing and supporting a very different sort of game, the upcoming platformer Rebounder. It's tough enough to stand out in the games market these days, let alone as a 2D platformer, so I'm always excited when one really breaks through and catches my eye. Rebounder is killing it on the art front, presenting everything in this color-limited, comic book, cel-shadey view that I really dig. It dovetails with the story and designs, a sort of blue collar, working class sci-fi reminiscent of Scavenger's Reign, Alien, or Mouthwashing. "On a remote lunar worksite, valuable resources from an ancient age flow underfoot, and shareholders demand extraction," reads Rebounders' synopsis on Steam. "Contract workers fly-in and fly-out; blue collar labourers from around the galaxy all trekking to the edges of civilization for the next gig. "A Rebounder runs lines. They pull up their boots each day…

title: Saber CCO says the studio isn't changing up its comms strategy after recent controversies: 'There's always some dust up'
summary: "The games will speak for themselves."
body: In a recent interview with PC Gamer's Joshua Wolens at this year's Gamescom, Saber Interactive CCO Tim Willits admitted the studio's leadership had a reputation for saying precisely what it means—"sometimes we 'say what we mean' too much," he laughed. But when asked if recent controversies would change the studio's comms approach, he said "no." "I've been in the industry for so long, and there's always some dust up," Willits explained. "People got mad at Saber because we put World War Z on Epic, and people were like, 'oh, Saber's destroying the industry.' Now 30 million people have played World War Z. And the games will speak for themselves, even in our experiment with Rideshare [Stimulator]." If you haven't been keeping up with the latest drama Saber Interactive has courted, here's the skinny: former Saber Interactive writer Stella Sacco claimed she was fired and replaced with AI during the development of Rideshare Stimulator. Saber's comms department initially put out a fairly benign statement disputing the details of the claim, but CEO Matt Karch subsequently issued a statement to This Week In Videogames that was both aggressively pro-AI, and personally insulting to Sacco. title: Dwarf Fortress co-creator Tarn Adams was amazed other devs had heard of his game the first time he went to a convention: 'I didn't know that anyone knew what we were doing'
summary: "I try to have good moral qualities, but I am apparently subject to all forms of flattery and vanity and such."
body: Dwarf Fortress is a bit like caviar—not everyone's into it, but the people who are describe their experiences with it like a religious awakening. But the game's legendary co-creator, Tarn Adams, didn't even know it had a big following for many years, as he told PC Gamer's Joshua Wolens in a recent interview at Gamescom 2026 . "It was something like 2013, 14 going to PAX in Seattle, and there was an indie mega booth at the time," he recalled. "Of the 50 or 60 games showing—I'm just ballparking the numbers—I'd say 90% of them heard of Dwarf Fortress and also had a very amazed fan-ish response when we were introduced." It was the first time Adams had a sense of the reach his game had. "That was crazy. I had no idea that that was even a thing," he said. "I didn't know that anyone knew what we were doing … I enjoyed it. I try to have good moral qualities, but I am apparently subject to all forms of flattery and vanity and such." If he could go back in time, he wouldn't so as to not "disrupt the timeline." title: Saber CCO Tim Willits blames layoffs on games industry overspecialization: 'Studios that have a couple hundred employees that work on one game are going to struggle'
summary: "Why not take a risk?"
body: With mega-games like GTA 6 on the way, it's hard not to feel like games are always getting bigger—both the software itself, and the teams that make it (GTA 6 has an entire dedicated NPC team "art-directing" its every background character). But in an interview with PC Gamer's Joshua Wolens, Saber Interactive CCO Tim Willits said a reliance on games with huge scopes and highly specialized teams may be responsible for some of the industry's many, many woes . "The industry always has some cycles, some ups and downs, and one of the things that we have done well to avoid some of the issues that other studios have had is we spread out our resources," Willits said. "We develop games that are across the scope spectrum, for lack of a better description." While games like Space Marine 2 and the upcoming Jurassic Park: Survival take a lot of manpower, the studio relies on remasters and smaller games to fund those "big bets." "We have a culture where people can work on any game, and we can move resources around. So we avoid the 'silo problem' that you find with big studios," he continued. title: Onimusha: Way of the Sword starts off slow, but stick with it: You'll be rewarded with some of the best action combat of the decade
summary: A slow gauntlet.
body: Play This Right Now Welcome to Play This Right Now, the site version of our weekly newsletter in which we celebrate a new game, update, or DLC that we think is well worth checking out. You can subscribe to the newsletter at the link if you want to get our thoughts about a new videogame happening direct to your inbox every Thursday. If you're sick of parrying in videogames, then Onimusha: Way of the Sword might hit you, dear reader, the wrong way—especially since its roll is extremely slow . The game's introduction to its combat is a competent, though incredibly careful one. It establishes its full suite of defensive abilities with a glacial pace. Like you're a deer and it's afraid you'll bolt into the underbrush. The problem with this is that it gives the wrong impression. Onimusha 's combat is utter action game bliss when it really gets going—but it takes a minute to get there. Not only does it drip-feed you with mechanics, but it starts off with the most ubiquitous one: The parry, or timed block, or deflect —whatever you want to call it. And listen, parry fatigue is widespread . In fact, one in four action game players has experienced it in the past five years alone. I get it. B…

title: Confession time: Alright, come clean—how tidy are your bags in your MMOs?
summary: Mine? Mine are an utter mess.
body: Terminally Online (Image credit: Future) This is Terminally Online : PC Gamer's very own MMO column. Every other week, I'll be sharing my thoughts on the genre, interviewing fellow MMO-heads like me, taking a deep-dive into mechanics we've all taken for granted, and, occasionally, bringing in guest writers to talk about their MMO of choice. Ah, the MMO inventory. The delightful abstraction that means we don't need to actually think all that hard about where to store the hundreds of thousands of pelts, steaks, teeth, claws, trinkets, coins, crystals, and so-on that we accrue. Our bags are full of crap, it is tradition . On the one hand, I'm grateful for it. I'm out here to grind and run dungeons, not try to Jenga-stack a briefcase Resident Evil-style. On the other hand, good lord does my head spin every time I open up my inventory and gaze upon the horrors of my own chronic lack of organisation. I despair. Please don't tell people how I live. (Image credit: Square Enix) I could argue that it's the game's fault. Giving me an auto-sorting feature means I can endure a descent into of disorganisation without much trouble. title: This free lockpicking puzzler you can play in your browser is unexpectedly one of the most thrilling games I've encountered this year
summary: Lockpicks-11 is a fiendish delight.
body: I love lockpicking minigames, especially when representatively they're as far away from the act of lockpicking as possible. While I admire the elegance of Bethesda's bobby-pin/screwdriver system seen in Fallout 4 , I'm much more interested in the weirder solutions like Splinter Cell 's baffling pin-flicking system, or Gothic Remake 's absurdly elaborate sliding puzzle system. I love how developers have tried so many ways to represent the act of lockpicking, and that despite this nobody has 'solved' the problem of virtual lockpicking yet (though Bethesda has arguably come closest). Inevitably, then, I was drawn to the idea of a game that is all about lockpicking. But I never expected that it could be as imaginative and thrilling as Lockpicks-11 . An entry for Ludum Dare 57, Lockpicks-11 places you in the role of an unnamed thief in the middle of a heist. Yet rather than being a fully fledged burglary simulator like Thief, Lockpicks-11 distils the act of larceny to a linear sequence of locked doors. What makes Lockpicks-11 interesting is that every lock is wildly different. Some are based upon recognisable locking mechanisms, like inputting a four digit code, or aligning symbols via…

title: Gaming monitors are one of the only good things about PC hardware right now, but one niche feature is underloved
summary: Doubling your refresh rate with just a few clicks? Yes please.
body: The memory crisis may be in full swing, taking numerous PC components with it, but the value of gaming monitors is one of a few hardware things that has actually improved over the last few years. In fact, their price-to-quality ratio is kind of outrageous right now, with even relatively recent QD-OLED screens going for around $300 . As such, monitors are one of the few things I check over without rolling my eyes, and therefore, they're one of a handful of techie bits that actually excites me. But that doesn't mean even they can't improve; when I chatted to gaming monitor brand AOC a few months ago, even its designers are aware the software isn't up to snuff. I've been testing out the Koorui G2741L, a dual mode 4K/1080p monitor, over the last few weeks, and all I can think is 'gosh, why aren't more companies doing dual mode,' and 'why aren't more companies doing dual mode better ?' The central argument for dual mode makes so much sense to me. When you want your games to look pretty, you swap to 4K at a lower refresh rate, and when you want something snappy and competitive, you drop it to 1080p with a much higher refresh rate.
